name: Brendan of Clonfert
knownFor: Irish founder of monasteries in the time of Columba of Iona, whom Adomnan names as Brendan Mocu Alti and whom later writers take to be the founder of Clonfert. Lives written centuries later make him the voyager who sought the Land of Promise.
dates: No source used here from near his own time gives a year. Adomnan places him in the lifetime of Columba of Iona. Wentworth Huyshe, Adomnan's translator, gives born 482, founded Clonfert 559 and died 577, without naming his source. Roderic O'Flaherty, as John O'Donovan quotes him, also gives 577
place: Ireland; the island of Hinba, where Adomnan says he visited Columba of Iona; Clonfert, which John O'Donovan places in county Galway. The Lismore Life says he was of the Ciarraige Luachra, of the Altraige Caille, and Wentworth Huyshe says Kerry was the chief district of his kin
role: Abbot and founder of monasteries; founder of Clonfert, as Wentworth Huyshe and later writers identify him

traces: The Annals of the Four Masters, in John O'Donovan's English, name bishops of "Clonfert-Brendan" from the 1170s on.
Roderic O'Flaherty, as John O'Donovan quotes him, says the cathedral of Enaghdun was dedicated to Saint Brendan, who died there.

The Book of Lismore keeps a story set at Clonfert, which Whitley Stokes calls the story of the harper and the bird-like angel. In it Brenainn maccu Altai has not smiled or heard worldly music for seven years.
remembered: The Catalogue of the Saints of Ireland, which Hugh Williams dates about 730, names two Brendans among the second order of Irish saints. It does not say which two.
The Stowe Missal, which Hugh Williams dates in its present form about 750, names a Brendinus twice among the priests it remembers.
The Lismore Life likens him to Abraham, David, Moses and Noah. As Noah raised the ark over the flood, it says, Brenainn will raise his monks and households over the fire of Doom.
John Mirk, an English preacher active about 1403, tells in a sermon for the feast of Matthias how Saint Brandan, at sea, found Judas sitting on a stone, let out of hell's heat at set times.
A Latin Life of David of Wales that W. J. Rees prints has Barre ride David's horse over the sea and meet Brendan living a wondrous life on a sea creature.

uncertain: Adomnan, a later abbot of Iona, is the earliest writer used here who names him, and he does so twice, in passing. Most of what is told of Brendan comes from Lives written centuries later. Whitley Stokes says the Book of Lismore was compiled in the later 1400s, and calls its language mixed, with Old Irish forms beside late Middle and even Modern ones. W. J. Rees thinks the Lives in his book were probably compiled about the twelfth century.

Which Brendan. Wentworth Huyshe takes Adomnan's Brendan Mocu Alti to be the founder of Clonfert, and Mocu Alti to be his clan name. The Lismore Life calls him son of Finnlug, of the Altraige, and Rees's Latin Life son of Finloc, grandson of Altus. Adomnan also tells of Brendan of Birr, who greeted Columba at a synod and whose death Columba saw in a vision. Huyshe says the two must be kept apart, and gives about 573 for the death of Brendan of Birr; John O'Donovan, from the Calendar of the O'Clerys, gives 572.
Two Brendans in the early lists. The Catalogue of the Saints of Ireland and the Stowe Missal each name two Brendans and do not say which is which.

His years. Huyshe gives 482 for his birth, 559 for the founding of Clonfert and 577 for his death, and names no source. Roderic O'Flaherty, as O'Donovan quotes him, gives 577 and says he died at Enaghdun. No annal with his death year is among the sources used here. The Annales Cambriae record only the death of Brendan of Birr.

The voyage. The Land of Promise is told by the late Lives. The Lismore Life has him sail five years, then seven, in three ships of hides, and at last reach the land in a great ship built in Connaught at Ita's word. Rees's Latin Life breaks off as the voyage is planned; Rees notes that the manuscript ends abruptly. Huyshe quotes a Latin Life of Brendan on how the voyagers built their boat of wicker and ox hides.

His feast. Huyshe gives his day as 16 May, and O'Flaherty, as O'Donovan quotes him, the 16th of May. The Lismore Life, in Whitley Stokes's English, places his festival on the seventh of the calends of June.

The link with Wales. Rees printed the Latin Life in the appendix of his Lives of the Cambro-British Saints. The saints there, he says, were not Cambro-British, but natives of Ireland who had passed much of their time in Wales. A Latin Life of Brendan that Hugh Williams quotes, after Warren, has Brendan at Gildas's monastery, singing Mass from a book in Greek letters.
